description: Fueled by the enthusiasm of Tech students in HCMC, our ambition in this challenge surpasses the boundaries of a contest. It is a playground for us to test our technical skills, maximize our problem solving potential, and gather precious experiences that will shape our path forward.
summary:
OrbitCraft 2D is a 2D pixel-art game that runs in a web browser. We built it for the "Space Mission Design Game" challenge. The player picks a mission (Earth orbit, the Moon, or Mars) and gets a budget and a science goal. Then they build a rocket and a spacecraft by dragging parts like engines, fuel tanks, fins, solar panels, batteries, antennas and science instruments. After that, they launch it and see what happens.
The game uses real physics to decide the result. It uses the rocket equation for delta-v, the thrust-to-weight ratio, rocket stability (center of gravity vs. center of pressure), and checks for power, heat and communication. Every change shows its effect right away, so players can see the trade-offs. For example, adding one more instrument makes the spacecraft heavier and means it needs more power.
After each flight, a report explains why the mission worked or failed. It shows which part caused the problem and how to fix it. There are 12 possible results.
This matters because most space games only show "win" or "lose." Ours teaches students why, using real NASA data.
details:
What It Does

OrbitCraft 2D is a 2D pixel-art game that runs in a web browser. The player is a space mission designer. They pick a mission, build a rocket and a spacecraft from parts, launch it, and then read a report that explains why the mission worked or failed.

There are three missions, from easy to hard:

  • Eyes on Earth (1 star): put an imaging satellite into Low Earth Orbit at 500 km. Budget $25M.
  • Lunar Prospector Jr. (2 stars): reach a 100 km orbit around the Moon and carry a spectrometer. Budget $40M.
  • Red Planet Scout (3 stars): reach a 400 km orbit around Mars with a camera and a spectrometer. Budget $70M.

Each mission has a budget, a delta-v (Δv) target, a distance from Earth and a science goal. The player has to meet all of them at once.

How It Works

The game has four steps.

1. Mission briefing. The player chooses a mission. Each mission starts with a ready-made design that has exactly one hidden flaw. The player has to find it and fix it. This teaches them how to play in a natural way.

2. Workshop. The player drags parts onto the rocket. There are 30 parts in 11 groups: nose cones, spacecraft frames (bus), science instruments, solar panels, batteries, thermal control, radios, fuel tanks, engines, fins and stage decouplers. The screen has three columns:

  • Parts bin on the left. Hovering a part shows its specs and its NASA source.
  • Blueprint in the middle. It shows the rocket, the Δv of each stage, and two markers: the center of gravity (CG) and the center of pressure (CP).
  • Live engineering data on the right. Each check has a meter that is green (pass), yellow (close to the limit) or red (will fail).

Every time the player changes a part, all the numbers update right away. The player can see what will break before they launch.

3. Test launch. The game simulates the flight and plays it as an animation. It shows time, altitude, speed, the current stage and a flight log.

4. Post-mortem report. After the flight, the report shows:

  • Root cause: what went wrong, explained with physics.
  • Parts involved: the parts that caused the problem.
  • How to fix: a suggestion.
  • Flight checks: the full list of checks, including problems that would have happened later.

The player presses "Fix in Workshop" to go back. The faulty parts flash red.

The flight checks

The simulator runs the checks in the same order as a real flight. The first check that fails is the root cause:

  1. Design review: are the parts put together correctly?
  2. Budget: is the total cost under the budget?
  3. Liftoff: is the thrust bigger than the weight (thrust-to-weight ratio > 1)?
  4. Stability: is the CP behind the CG? If not, the rocket tumbles.
  5. Δv to orbit: is there enough Δv to reach orbit?
  6. Δv transfer: is there enough Δv left to reach the Moon or Mars?
  7. Power: do the solar panels make enough power, and can the battery last through the dark part of the orbit (eclipse)?
  8. Thermal: can the spacecraft handle the heat and cold where it is going?
  9. Comms: can the radio reach Earth from this distance?
  10. Data: can the radio send all the data the instruments collect each day?
  11. Science: are the right instruments on board, with enough science points?

This gives 12 possible outcomes: invalid design, over budget, no liftoff, tumble, suborbital, stranded, dead battery, thermal failure, loss of signal, data bottleneck, not enough science, and mission success.

The physics behind it

The game does not use random numbers or scripted endings. Real formulas decide every result:

  • Tsiolkovsky rocket equation for the Δv of each stage, including dropping empty stages and the nose fairing.
  • Thrust-to-weight ratio at sea level. A vacuum engine gives no thrust at liftoff.
  • Barrowman method (from TIR-33) to find the center of pressure, plus the static stability margin in calibers.
  • Orbit math (Kepler's laws) to find the orbit period and how long the spacecraft is in Earth's shadow.
  • Inverse-square law for sunlight. At Mars, solar panels make only about 43% of their power at Earth.
  • Radio range and bandwidth. UHF works only near Earth, S-band reaches the Moon, and X-band reaches Mars.
  • The ion engine is very efficient but has very low thrust, so it gets a ×1.75 Δv penalty, the same idea as low-thrust paths in NASA's GMAT.

Stars and progress

Each mission can earn up to 3 stars:

  • 1 star for mission success.
  • 1 star for spending 80% of the budget or less.
  • 1 star for collecting 1.5 times the science goal.

Progress is saved in the browser, so players can come back later and try to get a better score.

Benefits

  • Learning by doing. Players learn engineering trade-offs by trying things and seeing what happens, not by reading.
  • It always explains why. Many space games only say "win" or "lose." Our game always names the cause, the parts at fault and the fix.
  • Instant feedback. The live meters and the CG/CP markers show the effect of every change, so players understand cause and effect.
  • Easy to start. It runs in any modern web browser. No install, no account, no special computer.
  • Based on real data. Parts and missions come from NASA documents, and each part shows its source.
  • Short sessions. One mission takes a few minutes, so it fits into a classroom lesson.

Intended Impact

Our main users are high school and university students, teachers, and anyone new to space science. Professional tools like NASA's GMAT are powerful but too hard for beginners. We want to fill the gap between a simple quiz and a professional tool.

We hope the game will:

  • Help students understand that space missions are about balance. One choice affects many others.
  • Teach real ideas like Δv, rocket stability, power budgets and communication range in a fun way.
  • Make players curious about engineering and space careers.
  • Give teachers a free tool they can use in class to explain rocket physics and mission planning.
  • Show that failure is part of engineering. Every failed launch teaches something useful.

Tools and Technologies

  • Language: JavaScript (ES modules).
  • Game engine: Phaser 4, for scenes, drawing, input and animation.
  • Build tool: Vite, for the development server and the production build.
  • Runtime for testing: Node.js 20+ with the built-in node:test runner. There are about 80 automated tests for physics, design rules, analysis, simulation, data, layout, art and scoring.
  • Graphics: all pixel art is drawn by code. There are no image files for parts.
  • Sound: retro sound effects made with the Web Audio API. There are no audio files.
  • Fonts: Silkscreen and VT323 pixel fonts (through Fontsource).
  • Storage: browser localStorage for progress and settings such as sound on/off.
  • Development process: GitHub Spec Kit for writing the spec, plan and tasks, with Claude Code as an AI coding assistant. We also used Git, VS Code and Python (to run Spec Kit).
  • Hardware: only normal laptops. The game needs no special hardware.

Data sources:

  • NASA Small Spacecraft Technology State-of-the-Art 2024 (spacecraft classes, instruments, power, radios, ion engine).
  • NASA Venture Class Launch Services (small rocket sizes, engines, costs).
  • TIR-33, Calculating the Center of Pressure of a Model Rocket (stability).
  • NASA Small Spacecraft Systems Virtual Institute, Thermal Control (thermal parts).
  • NASA GMAT (mission types and Δv budgets).

Code design

We kept the game logic separate from the display:

  • src/data: parts and missions.
  • src/core: pure logic for physics, design checks, analysis, simulation and scoring. It does not depend on Phaser, so we can test it with Node.
  • src/scenes, src/ui, src/art: screens, widgets, sound and pixel art.

Because of this, we can change the numbers and run the tests to make sure every mission can still be solved.

Creativity

  • Post-mortem instead of game over. Each failure becomes a short lesson with a cause, the parts at fault and a fix. The faulty parts flash red in the workshop.
  • The "domino effect." Players can watch one change spread through the system: a heavier instrument means less Δv and more power needed, which means more solar panels, which adds mass and cost.
  • Predicted failures. The report also shows problems that would have happened later in the flight, so players can fix everything at once.
  • Starter designs with one flaw. Each mission starts with a design that is almost right. This works as a puzzle and as a tutorial.
  • Visible physics. The CG and CP markers on the rocket turn an abstract idea into something players can see and move.
  • Everything made in code. The art and sound are generated by code, so the game is small, loads fast and has a consistent retro style.
  • Real sources in the game. Each part tells you which NASA document its numbers come from.

Factors We Considered

  • Challenge requirements. The challenge asks for a game that covers mission goals, spacecraft design, science instruments, launch vehicle, budget, power, mass, communications and orbit. Every one of these is a real check in our game.
  • Scientific accuracy vs. simplicity. We used real formulas but kept the number of parts small and the rules clear. We only use the stability check during the early flight in the atmosphere, which matches the limits of the TIR-33 method.
  • Difficulty curve. The three missions get harder step by step. Each one teaches a new idea: stability at Earth, communication at the Moon, and weak sunlight and long distance at Mars.
  • Accessibility. The game runs in a browser, has full keyboard shortcuts, undo/redo, a help screen, tooltips on every part and meter, and a mute button.
  • Clear feedback. Colors (green, yellow, red), simple messages and fix suggestions help beginners understand what to do.
  • Performance and size. No large image or sound files, so the game loads fast even on slow internet and older computers.
  • Reliability. Automated tests check the physics and make sure every mission can be completed.
  • Honest data. Every part names its source, so players and teachers can look up the real numbers.
  • Replay value. Stars for saving money and extra science give players a reason to improve their designs.
